HR@10 with one positive and 99 unique negatives measures success within a 100-item candidate set, not full-catalog top-10 retrieval. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; fixed candidates improve comparability but do not remove sampling bias. Keep the pinned evaluator and describe results explicitly as sampled-candidate validation HR@10. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For uncertainty reporting, a suitable application of paired evaluation is to retain each user’s binary hit for both models, resample matched user pairs within each category, and recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. Report the observed difference and a descriptive 95% paired-bootstrap interval alongside category scores. This preserves pairing and macro weighting. With 200 users/category, one changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. Such intervals condition on fitted checkpoints and fixed candidate sets; they exclude training-seed and negative-sampling variability. [Paired evaluation tests](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=744), [Bootstrap confidence intervals](https://www.nist.gov/publications/computing-confidence-intervals-common-ir-measures)

Repeated checkpoint and trial selection on the same validation panel creates optimism: the winning score benefits from validation noise. Bootstrapping only the selected winner does not correct this adaptive selection, and ordinary pairwise intervals do not establish significance across the search. Report search breadth, selection rule, and validation improvements as exploratory; reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s independent held-out evaluation after selection is frozen. Multiple-comparison corrections for prespecified comparisons alone do not resolve unrestricted adaptive reuse. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
